documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT), Academic Integrity
documents.title: NavigateAI Use at CSU: What's allowed, When to ask, and What to avoid
documents.summary: A student-facing trail-map guide that sorts AI uses into open, permission-required and closed zones. Learning uses are encouraged; credit work needs instructor permission; fully generated work and exam use are misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The guide gives three named tiers and says "Every guide runs their trail differently" and AI for credit work "requires their explicit permission". It sets no single rule and hands the decision to instructors, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: The guide sorts AI use into three zones: "Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed". This is a named tier scheme, so P05 (named tiers), not P04, because the tiers are fixed categories.
units.anchor: some require special permits, and some are closed because the paths are perilous
units.frag_start: Some paths are open to everyone

units.why: Under "Trail Open" the text says "You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery". It welcomes AI for learning uses, so P02 (encourage), though only for ungraded learning activities.
units.anchor: You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery
units.frag_start: You are encouraged to use AI
units.fit_note: Encouragement applies only to the listed learning activities, not to graded work.

units.why: "Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way" allows AI as an explainer of course concepts, which is the tutor use in P12.
units.anchor: Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way.
units.frag_start: Use AI to explain a complex

units.why: "Explore concepts related to your course" with a list of key figures or debates is general topic exploration, like a search engine, so P12 (understand concepts) fits better than P15 (brainstorming approaches).
units.anchor: Explore concepts related to your course.
units.frag_end: main debates in a scientific field.

units.why: "Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam" is a study-aid use, matching P14.
units.anchor: Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam.

units.why: "AI tools can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations)" warns that output may be wrong, which is the P31 verify rule.
units.anchor: AI tools can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations).
units.frag_start: AI tools can sometimes lead you

units.why: "You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work" puts the duty to check output on the student. I chose P31 (verify) over P29 (ownership) because the stated duty is verification.
units.anchor: You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work.
units.frag_start: You are always responsible for verifying

units.why: "Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission" sets the fallback: AI on credit work is not allowed unless the instructor permits it. That is P06 in effect, and it is a restrict stance.
units.anchor: Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission.
units.fit_note: States the default as permission-required for credit work; it does not use the word 'silent'.

units.why: "asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment" and "Every guide runs their trail differently" leave the decision to each instructor and assignment, which is P04.
units.anchor: Every guide runs their trail differently.

units.why: Students must "Check with your instructor before using AI to help you" write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report or paper. The permission is per instructor, so P04 rather than a ban.
units.anchor: Write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.
units.policy: Students check with the instructor before using AI to write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.
units.fit_note: Not banned: it needs the instructor's permission first.

units.why: "Outline or organize your arguments for a graded assignment" is on the same "Check with your instructor" list, so each instructor decides (P04).
units.anchor: Outline or organize your arguments for a graded assignment.
units.policy: Students check with the instructor before using AI to outline or organize their arguments for a graded assignment.
units.fit_note: Needs the instructor's permission first rather than being banned.

units.why: "Generate code or solve problems for credit" is on the permit-required list, so AI code generation for credit is allowed only with instructor permission. This is the computing-relevant item, assigned P04 because permission is case by case.
units.anchor: Generate code or solve problems for credit.
units.policy: Students check with the instructor before using AI to generate code or solve problems for credit.
units.fit_note: Not banned outright; the instructor may permit it.

units.why: "Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment" is also listed under "Check with your instructor", so take-home work depends on instructor permission (P04), unlike in-class exams.
units.anchor: Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.
units.policy: Students check with the instructor before using AI to complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.
units.fit_note: Needs instructor permission rather than being banned.

units.why: "When in doubt, ask your guide" tells students to ask the instructor when unsure, the P10 rule.
units.anchor: When in doubt, ask your guide.
units.frag_start: When in doubt, ask your guide.

units.why: "An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct" classes AI use without permission as misconduct, which is P36.
units.anchor: An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct.

units.why: "Entering it is a violation of CSU’s Academic Integrity Policy" classes the listed AI uses as integrity violations, so P36. It does not state a penalty, so P37 does not apply.
units.anchor: Entering it is a violation of CSU’s Academic Integrity Policy
units.policy: The listed AI uses are a violation of CSU's Academic Integrity Policy and misrepresent the student's own learning and effort.

units.why: "This applies to anything considered “work for credit” (graded, pass/fail, or marked as completed)" defines what work the rules cover, a scope definition (P61).
units.anchor: This applies to anything considered “work for credit”
units.fit_note: Defines scope as 'work for credit' rather than defining AI.

units.why: "Turning in an essay, lab report, or any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI" is submitting AI-made work as one's own, P19, classed as misconduct.
units.anchor: Turning in an essay, lab report, or any other assignment that was fully generated by

units.why: "Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam" bans all AI use on quizzes and exams (P22), with "in any way" making it total.
units.anchor: Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam.
units.frag_start: Using an AI tool in any way

units.why: "Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up in a research paper or bibliography" forbids submitting fabricated material. I chose P74 (fabrication) over P31 because it is listed as misconduct, not as advice to check.
units.anchor: Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up

units.why: "Using AI to rewrite or “spin” sentences or paragraphs from a source and presenting them as your own original summary" is AI-produced text submitted as own work (P19), and also a plagiarism form.
units.anchor: Using AI to rewrite or “spin” sentences or paragraphs from a source
units.fit_note: Specifically AI paraphrasing of a source ('patchwriting') presented as one's own summary.

units.why: "Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment where your instructor has explicitly asked you to declare it" makes nondisclosure itself the violation, P28.
units.anchor: Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment

units.why: "Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them as your own work" names code and solutions explicitly, so P19 (do not have AI produce submitted work).
units.anchor: Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them as your own work

units.why: "building the strength and skill that only come from the climb (the learning process)" gives the reason for limits: doing the work builds skill, which is P41.
units.anchor: building the strength and skill that only come from the climb
units.frag_start: The goal of an assignment isn’t just

units.why: "How do I credit my AI Tools (when allowed)? Visit the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide" points students to a citation guide when AI is allowed. It supports P24 (disclose and cite) but gives no rule itself.
units.anchor: Visit the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide
units.frag_start: Visit the CSU Library's AI Citation
units.fit_note: Only points to a library guide; it states no citation requirement.

units.why: "The content and framework were developed by the CSU Academic Integrity Program" says who made the guide and how, which is P84.
units.anchor: The content and framework were developed by the CSU Academic Integrity Program.

units.why: "We used a large language model as a collaborative partner to help brainstorm analogies, refine the language" discloses the office's own AI use in making the guide. P48 (disclose AI-made materials) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: We used a large language model as a collaborative partner
units.frag_start: We used a large language model
units.fit_note: Disclosure by the policy authors of AI in drafting the guide, not by an instructor about course materials.

units.why: "Who decides what is acceptable and unacceptable assistance (help) on an assignment, essay, or exam? The simple answer is the instructor." Instructors set the rule, so P04.
units.anchor: Because the instructor of a course decides what is acceptable and unacceptable help
units.frag_start: Because the instructor of a course
units.frag_end: unacceptable help, the expectation can change from course to course.
units.fit_note: Stated about help on graded work in general, not only AI.

units.why: "the expectation can change from course to course" says each course's rules differ and one course's permission does not carry over, matching P11.
units.anchor: the expectation can change from course to course
units.fit_note: Stated for help on graded work in general, with a partner-work example, not only AI.

documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT)
documents.title: Crafting Syllabus Statements on Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
documents.summary: Faculty guidance on writing short syllabus AI statements, with four sample statements and advice on teaching AI literacies. It says a campus-wide policy is unlikely to fit and leaves rules to instructors.
documents.stance_why: It offers sample statements from prohibitive to permissive and says "it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs", urging instructors to use their "best judgment". It sets no stance of its own, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: The guide says it is "intended to help faculty ... create concise, effective, and purpose-driven syllabus statements" on AI. It asks instructors to put AI expectations in the syllabus, which is P09 as guidance.
units.anchor: create concise, effective, and purpose-driven syllabus statements about the use of generative artificial intelligence
units.frag_start: This guide is intended to help
units.fit_note: Offered as guidance to faculty, not as a mandate.

units.why: "They guide: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding" explains why statements exist; it is the purpose of P09-type statements.
units.anchor: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding
units.fit_note: Gives a reason for having statements rather than requiring them.

units.why: "they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course and, then, justification for our intervention" says the statement is the basis for later enforcement. No existing type covers statements as grounds for action, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course
units.uncovered_note: A syllabus AI statement serves as the stated expectation that justifies later intervention for misconduct.

units.why: "Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI and how they are allowed to use it" tells instructors to write clear statements; P09.
units.anchor: Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI and how they are

units.why: The first question a good statement answers is "What is the scope of the policy? Does it cover all course activities or only graded work?" Instructors should state scope in the statement, so P09.
units.anchor: Does it cover all course activities or only graded work?
units.fit_note: Asks the writer to state the scope; the requirement to have a statement is implied.

units.why: "State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do" tells instructors to list permitted and prohibited uses in the statement (P09).
units.anchor: State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do.

units.why: "a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here" tells instructors to link a color-coded framework of AI-use levels, so P05.
units.anchor: If you plan to use a clarifying resource, a color-coded chart or other guide, reference
units.frag_start: If you plan to use a

units.why: "Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you" has instructors invite questions about the AI rule, which is P66 (discuss rules with students).
units.anchor: Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you.

units.why: The prohibitive sample: "You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit in this course." A ban on credit work, so P01.
units.anchor: You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit
units.frag_start: You may NOT use AI when
units.frag_end: work for credit in this course.
units.fit_note: Offered as a sample statement instructors may adopt, not as university policy.

units.why: The same sample adds "You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material, concepts", which allows AI for understanding and study. P12 fits better than P14 because investigating concepts comes first.
units.anchor: You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material, concepts, etc.
units.frag_start: You MAY use it to investigate,

units.why: "Here is a color-coded framework that we will be using to help make this distinction clearer" in the prohibitive sample shows a colour-coded framework of uses, P05.
units.anchor: Here is a color-coded framework that we will be using to help make this distinction

units.why: The conditional sample: "You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways." AI is allowed only for listed uses, so restrict; the type is P04 since the instructor sets uses per assignment.
units.anchor: You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways.
units.frag_start: You may only use generative AI
units.fit_note: Allowed only in specific ways set by the framework, not blanket permission.

units.why: "we will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment at the time it is introduced" sets the rule per assignment, P04.
units.anchor: we will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment at
units.frag_start: we will discuss how you may

units.why: The limited-use sample: "You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class except on assignments that I have explicitly identified." AI is banned unless named, the fallback in P06.
units.anchor: You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class except
units.frag_start: You are not authorized to use

units.why: "On those assignments, you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use of such technologies" has the instructor guide students on identified assignments, which is P35 (assignment-specific AI interaction).
units.anchor: you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use of such technologies
units.fit_note: Promises guidance on assignments where AI is allowed rather than redesigning grading.

units.why: "You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies in any other facet of this course" says permission on one assignment does not extend elsewhere, P11.
units.anchor: You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies in any
units.fit_note: Limits permission to the named assignments within one course, not between courses.

units.why: The accountability sample says "The use of generative AI tools is broadly permitted in this course to help you brainstorm, draft, and revise your work." AI is welcomed with conditions, so P02.
units.anchor: The use of generative AI tools is broadly permitted in this course to help you
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI tools
units.fit_note: Also names brainstorming, drafting and revising as permitted uses.

units.why: "authentic engagement means you are fully accountable for the final submission" makes the student responsible for what they hand in, P29.
units.anchor: you are fully accountable for the final submission

units.why: "Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy" requires checking output, P31.
units.anchor: Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy.

units.why: "Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects your own understanding" requires students to make the work their own. P29 (own what you submit) fits better than P32.
units.anchor: Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects your own understanding.

units.why: "Cite your use of the AI tool following the guidance in the CSU Library's Guidelines for Acknowledging AI Use in Research" requires citation, P24.
units.anchor: Cite your use of the AI tool following the guidance in the
units.frag_start: Cite your use of the AI

units.why: "Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work ... will result in a poor grade" states a consequence in advance, P37.
units.anchor: will result in a poor grade.
units.fit_note: Penalty is only 'a poor grade'; it also says such work fails integrity standards.

units.why: "Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively, gaining fluency in their features and applications" asks faculty to teach AI use as a skill, P44.
units.anchor: Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively, gaining fluency in their features and

units.why: "Encourage students to evaluate AI’s strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts" asks faculty to build critical literacy. P44 (teach AI use) is nearest; it also touches P53.
units.anchor: Encourage students to evaluate AI’s strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts
units.fit_note: Critical evaluation of AI and its societal impacts, not only effective use.

units.why: "Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts" asks faculty to teach judgment about when AI is appropriate, P44.
units.anchor: Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts
units.fit_note: Judgment about when to use AI and adapting its output, not just tool fluency.

units.why: "Generative AI offers exciting possibilities for learning but also raises valid concerns about academic integrity and critical thinking, environmental impact, unevenly distributed access" names harms and access concerns, P53.
units.anchor: valid concerns about academic integrity and critical thinking, environmental impact, unevenly distributed access
units.fit_note: Also names unequal access, which P51 covers.

units.why: "it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs and concerns" says CSU will not set one campus rule and leaves AI rules to courses, P04.
units.anchor: it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs and concerns
units.frag_end: concerns that have and will arise.
units.fit_note: Gives the reason for delegating: usefulness of AI varies by course.

units.why: "You are urged to use your best judgment and to update your syllabus languages your ideas change" asks instructors to revise their statements over time, P54.
units.anchor: to update your syllabus languages your ideas change
units.frag_start: You are urged to use your

units.why: "Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community" points instructors to disciplinary norms when setting AI rules. No type covers this, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should consult their discipline's standards on AI when writing their own policy.

units.why: "The right statement for your course will depend on your specific learning objectives" ties the AI rule to learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: The right statement for your course will depend on your specific learning objectives

units.why: "How am I ensuring that the use of AI in my course promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking and learning" asks instructors to check that AI supports thinking. Nearest is P41, which protects skill-building.
units.anchor: promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking and learning
units.fit_note: Framed as a reflective question to instructors rather than a limit on students.

units.why: "This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT)" and "The final content reflects human review" disclose AI in drafting the guidance and its human review, P48.
units.anchor: This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT)
units.fit_note: Disclosure by the guide's authors; covers drafting and human review of guidance.

documents.title: Policies & Resources (Academic Integrity section)
documents.summary: The CS department page includes one sentence on generative AI in its academic-integrity list. It names turning in generative-AI work as one's own as clearly unacceptable and gives no permitted uses.
documents.stance_why: The only AI text is "Turning in work created by generative AI as one’s own" listed under "clearly unacceptable behaviors". It bans AI-made submissions and permits nothing, so prohibit, though the scope is narrow.

units.why: The department lists "Turning in work created by generative AI as one’s own" under "Examples of clearly unacceptable behaviors". Submitting AI-made work as one's own is P19, and the list classes it as dishonesty.
units.anchor: Turning in work created by generative AI as one’s own.
units.frag_start: Turning in work created by generative
units.policy: Turning in work created by generative AI as one's own is clearly unacceptable behavior in the CS Department.

notes: Coder B. The CS department page has one AI sentence; other academic-integrity text there (explain your solution, similarity) is not AI-specific and was not coded. The NavigateAI page repeats its text twice; coded once. The Course Hero and study-site FAQ was not coded (no AI content).
